summary: Gives guidelines for IETF working groups that choose to use GitHub for their work. It is informational, and it does not change IETF process rules.

eli5.summary: Groups that write Internet rules sometimes use a website for sharing drafts and ideas. This document gives them tips on how to work together there smoothly.

subtitle: Best practices for IETF working groups using GitHub for standards development.

tldr.problem: IETF working groups want to use GitHub to manage documents and track issues, but lack guidance on how to integrate it into their processes while maintaining transparency and consensus.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides policies and best practices for organizing repositories, managing contributions, using issue tracking, handling pull requests, and assessing consensus on GitHub.
tldr.outcome: Working groups can use GitHub effectively to improve document quality and participation while remaining consistent with IETF processes and RFC 2418 working group guidelines.

facts.label: Required files
facts.value: README, CONTRIBUTING, IETF Note Well citation

today: RFC 8874 is an Informational RFC providing guidance to IETF working groups. It remains the definitive reference for GitHub usage practices in the IETF, and is often cited by working group chairs establishing GitHub policies.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
GitHub is a widely used platform for hosting code repositories and collaborating on projects. IETF working groups have increasingly adopted GitHub to manage Internet-Draft development, taking advantage of features like version control, issue tracking, and pull requests.

GitHub can improve working group processes by increasing transparency, broadening community participation, and reducing the time needed to produce documents. However, effective use of GitHub requires clear policies and agreement within the working group.

This document provides guidelines for working groups that choose to use GitHub, covering administrative setup, contribution methods, and how to maintain consensus-driven decision-making while leveraging GitHub's collaborative tools.
sections.eli5: GitHub helps working groups work together better by tracking changes and discussions, but the group needs clear rules about how to use it.

sections.title: Administrative Setup and Policies
sections.content:
A working group using GitHub SHOULD create a dedicated GitHub organization named consistently, such as ietf-wg-NAME where NAME is the working group name. This organization MUST have at least two owners: responsible area directors and the IETF Secretariat. Working group chairs SHOULD also be included as owners.

Repositories SHOULD be created per document (one document per repository) rather than bundling multiple documents, as this reduces overhead and keeps work focused. Repository names SHOULD indicate adoption status; for instance, names starting with draft-ietf- indicate an adopted working group item.

Each working group MUST publish its GitHub policies clearly. These should be documented in the repository's README or CONTRIBUTING file, and linked from the working group charter. Policies MUST include citations to the IETF Note Well.

Working group chairs are responsible for deciding which GitHub features (issue tracking, pull requests, continuous integration) the group will formally use and communicating these decisions to the working group mailing list.
sections.eli5: The working group creates an organization on GitHub, sets up repositories for its documents, and writes down its rules.

sections.title: Contribution Methods
sections.content:
GitHub provides multiple ways to contribute: issues, pull requests, and inline comments. Editors MUST be given write access to repositories. Other contributors can use pull requests and issues without write access by creating a fork.

Issues track problems, discussions, and tasks. They can be labeled (for example, as "editorial" or "design") and assigned to contributors. A working group MUST decide whether issues are used only for recording items or as venues for substantive technical discussion.

Pull requests propose specific changes. Editors are encouraged to use pull requests for substantial changes rather than committing directly, as this creates a record of decisions and allows others to review changes. Editors SHOULD be permitted to merge pull requests at their discretion, though chairs may request that controversial pull requests wait for working group consensus.

Working group chairs MUST decide who is permitted to close issues and under what conditions. Early in a document's life, restrictions are generally not helpful. As documents mature, chairs may require that substantive issues be discussed on the mailing list before closing.
sections.eli5: People can propose changes using pull requests, discuss problems in issues, and label them so everyone knows what they're about.

sections.title: GitHub Usage Modes
sections.content:
The RFC describes three main modes of working group GitHub usage, progressing from lightweight to more involved:

Document Management Mode: GitHub is used only for managing document versions and editing. Substantive discussion happens on the working group mailing list. Issues and pull requests may exist but have no formal standing in the decision process.

Issue Tracking Mode: The working group records outstanding issues in the issue tracker to track state and resolution, but substantive discussion always occurs on the mailing list. Editors may resolve editorial issues on GitHub, but anything substantial MUST be discussed via email. This mode maintains compatibility with existing working group practices.

Issue Discussion Mode: Substantive technical discussion occurs on GitHub issues. Decisions are still confirmed on the mailing list before being finalized, especially for contentious matters and milestones like Working Group Last Call. This mode is more flexible but requires more GitHub discipline.

Working groups can adopt different modes for different documents or phase in stricter processes as documents mature. For instance, early design phases might use loose Issue Discussion Mode, transitioning to Issue Tracking Mode once a document is stable.
sections.eli5: Groups can choose how much they use GitHub: just for filing changes, for tracking issues plus email discussion, or for full discussions on GitHub as long as they confirm on email later.

sections.title: Assessing Consensus and Decision-Making
sections.content:
Working group chairs remain the arbiters of consensus, even when GitHub is used extensively. GitHub facilitates discussion and creates transparency, but consensus MUST ultimately be confirmed using the working group mailing list.

GitHub activity may not reach all interested participants. Some participants follow only emails or attend meetings, not GitHub. Chairs MUST consult the mailing list for potentially contentious issues to ensure a wider audience is heard.

Important milestones such as Working Group Last Call MUST involve the mailing list to ensure the widest possible review. Labels can be used to mark issues with formal consensus (for instance, a "has-consensus" label), making the status clear to all contributors.

Issues MUST NOT be reopened unless new information is presented. For long-running work, this prevents rehashing of previously resolved contentious discussions.
sections.eli5: Chairs still decide what the group agrees on, and they have to check the email list even if discussion happened on GitHub.

sections.title: Best Practices for Editors
sections.content:
Document editors are the primary maintainers and can improve the process through good practices:

  • Accept contributions from new contributors generously. Rather than rejecting a pull request with errors, accept it and fix issues afterward to encourage participation.
  • Never close an issue or pull request without understanding why it was opened. Explain every action clearly and courteously.
  • When a comment raises a new issue, create an issue or pull request to capture it rather than letting it be forgotten in a comment.
  • Provide change logs summarizing substantive changes in each Internet-Draft revision so contributors can follow activity.
  • Respond promptly to pull requests and issues to maintain momentum.

These practices lower barriers to entry and foster a welcoming community, ultimately improving document quality.
sections.eli5: Editors should be friendly, welcome contributions, and keep good notes of what changed and why.
